extracted_by: hand, T-0309 — the Democrat read, December 1833
note: Vol. I No. 4. A quiet week whose value is in ADDRESSES: four advertisements new to the corpus each locate themselves against something already documented — Montgomery's boot and shoe shop next door to Philo Carpenter's store, G. Spring's office second door west from the corner of Franklin and South Water, J. D. Caton's one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co., and Wentworth's tavern eighteen miles out on the Ottawa road. That is a chain of relative placements along one frontage, which is worth more to a reconstruction than four unplaced trades. The rest of the issue is the standing advertising already read at 1833-11-26 and 1833-12-03, the December town ordinances reprinted, and national and literary reprint on pages 1, 2 and 4; none of it is re-claimed. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST: the sweep returns the page-1 agent list of out-of-county postmasters and two national paragraphs about the Post Master General, and no list. Zero printed, zero extracted.

claims.notes: THE TAVERN KEEPER MARRIES. Chester Ingersoll is the man who took 'that noted Tavern Stand in Chicago, lately occupied by Mr. Wm. Wattles' and renamed it the Traveller's Home (T-0308 c006), and he is also one of the two judges of the election notice in the same first number (T-0308 c004). This ties the household to the house: on 12 December 1833 the keeper of one of the town's inns married Betsy Weaver, by the same magistrate who married the Nobles and the Bickerdykes a fortnight before (1833-12-03 c007). Four Chicago weddings in three weeks, every one of them performed by R. J. Hamilton, is also a claim about how few officiants the town had.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S DRUGGIST SELLS TEMPERANCE ALMANACS, AND THE TOWN HAS A TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. A week later the Chicago Temperance Society advertises a discourse at the Baptist Meeting House (1833-12-24 c001), and John Watkins signs as its secretary. Carpenter's stock of almanacs is the commercial end of the same movement and dates it: temperance is organised in Chicago by December 1833. As a claim about the fabric it adds only that Carpenter's shop is trading; his address stays unrecorded.

claims.notes: THE FINEST-GRAINED PLACEMENT IN THE DECEMBER SET: SECOND DOOR WEST FROM A NAMED CORNER. Franklin and South Water is a real intersection the plat carries, and 'second door west' is a countable position along the frontage — the kind of address a reconstruction can actually use, because it fixes the side of the street and the order of the shopfronts on it. THE ADVERTISER'S NAME IS LOST at the head of the advertisement ('ae = NG.') and is supplied from the gazetteer's later reading of G. Spring at the same trade and the same form of address; the quote carries no name and this note says so. The Chicago Academy stands on the same corner (1833-12-03 c015), so Franklin and South Water carries two documented occupants in December 1833.

claims.notes: THE ROAD TO OTTAWA HAS A STAGE HOUSE ON IT BY DECEMBER 1833, AND IT IS EIGHTEEN MILES OUT. That is a claim about the country the town sat in rather than about the town: Chicago's southwestern road was carrying enough travellers to keep an inn a day's wagon-haul away, stocked with corn and oats for their teams. The house is already in this corpus's gazetteer twice over from later readings; this advertisement is its OPENING, and 'has opened' dates it to the week of 17 December 1833.

claims.notes: THE ADDRESS THAT PLACES TWO BUSINESSES AT ONCE. Caton is the man ordinance 14 appointed attorney for the corporation of Chicago at the sitting of 4 December (1833-12-10 c007); two weeks later he advertises an office one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co. on South Water Street. Brewster, Hogan & Co. take three advertisements in this month and give an address in none of them, so this card is what puts the largest new firm of December 1833 on the town's principal frontage. Read with G. Spring's 'second door west from the corner of Franklin and South Water' (c005), South Water Street in December 1833 carries at least five documented doorways: the Democrat's office and Kimball's store at the Clark corner, Peck's at the La Salle corner, Brewster Hogan's, and Caton's beside it.

claims.notes: A DEATH IN THE PRINTER'S FAMILY, AND THE COUNTY'S PROBATE MACHINERY WORKING. The Democrat's editor and proprietor is John Calhoun; Samuel Calhoun's estate is administered in the same month in the same paper, and the corpus does not establish the relation, so none is asserted. What the notice does document is that Cook county has a Court of Probate, a Judge of Probate with an office, and a standing PUBLIC administrator — J. B. Beaubien — nine months before the scene year. Institutions are as much a part of a town as its buildings and this corpus records very few of them.

claims.notes: AN ESTRAY OX, DESCRIBED EAR BY EAR. The value of these notices is that nothing else in the record describes a working animal this closely: a yellowish brindle ox of about six years, lighter in the face, white-bellied, one horn topped, both ears cropped and slit — eighteen dollars. It also names five more men living in Cook county in December 1833 and puts Isaac Harmon on the bench as a justice of the peace; he is the same Isaac Harmon who attests the town ordinances as clerk of the Board of Trustees (1833-12-24 c010), so one man is both the corporation's clerk and a county magistrate.
